source.title: The Importance of Being Scalable: Improving the Speed and Accuracy of Neural Network Interatomic Potentials Across Chemical Domains

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in neural network interatomic potentials, a non-language domain, using model and training-data scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the log-log training-data-size slopes in Figure 6 and the reported OC20 scaling sweeps in Figure 8. Benchmark comparisons, efficiency results, rotational-equivariance tests, and other molecular/material datasets are not results on the power-law scaling behavior relevant to the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper for neural network interatomic potentials (EScAIP). Its scaling sweeps exist to show that the model 'scales well'. They are not tests of power-law form. Fig 6 fits log-log slopes over only a 4x range of data (25–100% of OC20 2M), with four points and no fit quality. Fig 8 spans 500k to 172M samples, but the text only says error 'consistently decreases'. It fits no power law, and epochs differ (30 vs 8). Neither can show whether the V5 power-law form holds. The results bear on 'error falls with data and model size', not on the power-law claim, so no verdict is given.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors argue that domain constraints such as built-in equivariance hinder NNIP scaling, and that adding attention parameters is the most effective way to scale. EScAIP is state of the art on OC20, OC22, MPTrj, SPICE and MD22, 10x faster with 5x less memory, and learns rotational equivariance from data. They also say error improves as model and data size grow, but they do not claim or fit a power law.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns neural network interatomic potentials and energy/force MAE, not language-model held-out cross-entropy; it studies data-size and architecture scaling rather than compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported data-scaling slopes vary by parameter-scaling configuration and rotation order L; the authors describe More AT as having steeper force-MAE slopes than AT + SC and the original L=6 model.

fits_no_version.finding: In EquiformerV2 on OC20 2M, the log-log data-scaling slope of force MAE depends on where parameters are added at matched size: More AT about -0.40, AT+SC -0.32, original L=6 -0.28.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In atomistic potentials, the data-scaling exponent depends on architecture and parameter allocation, not only on parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: At about 84M parameters, EquiformerV2 variants (different L and allocations) span force MAE 19.87–21.63 meV/Å and energy MAE 274–283 meV (Fig 2). The authors say many are comparable to L=6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In NNIPs, at fixed parameter count, architecture details (rotation order, attention vs channels) change error modestly. This is an analogue of V4 outside language models.

record.problems: The paper states that computational cost prevented error bars for every experiment. The OC20 scaling-sweep values are presented in figures, and the text gives qualitative trends rather than a complete set of numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Other reported results concern benchmark accuracy, efficiency, rotational equivariance, or separate datasets and do not directly test the versions recorded here.

untested.parts: No power-law fit over several orders of magnitude of data, parameters or compute for NNIPs. No image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer regimes.
Not language models (see fits_no_version for the NNIP analogue).
No downstream-vs-scale analysis in the sense of the claim.
No analysis of fitting-choice dependence of published laws.

missing.what: EScAIP model-size trend at fixed data. OC20 All+MD val force MAE is 15.07/12.82/12.17 meV/Å for 83M/146M/317M (Small/Medium/Large); OC20 2M is 20.15/19.08. Under 1 order of magnitude, no fit.
Parameter-matched ablation of EquiformerV2 allocations (force and energy MAE with parameter counts).

record.verdict_notes: A NeurIPS 2024 architecture paper. The scaling evidence is illustrative (monotone improvement, a short-range log-log slope) rather than a test of power-law form. No error bars, and compute is not varied as an axis. The reader's 'supports V5' label is dropped because no row can show a power law.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits are used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is studied.
The study does not test whether language-model architecture details have little effect at fixed parameter count.

Tests atomistic potential errors against training-data size and reports performance changes across model sizes, but does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as scaling regimes, nor power laws against compute.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship to language-model pretraining loss is measured.
The study does not assess fitting-choice dependence or curve bending for language-model scaling laws.
